title: How to Calculate Your FIRE Number (Financial Independence Retire Early)
description: The math behind the movement: Using the '25x Rule' to determine when work becomes optional.
content:
Financial Independence, Retire Early (FIRE) is not just a trend; it is a mathematical framework. The core question every aspiring early retiree asks is: 'What is my number?' How much money do you need invested so that you never have to work for a paycheck again? The answer lies in the relationship between your annual spending and your safe withdrawal rate. This guide breaks down the '4% Rule,' how to calculate your specific FIRE number, and the variables that might force you to adjust it.

Key Takeaways

  • The Formula: Annual Expenses x 25 = Your FIRE Number. If you spend $40,000/year, you need $1,000,000. If you spend $100,000, you need $2.5 Million.
  • The 4% Rule: This rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio in Year 1, adjust for inflation every subsequent year, and have a 95% chance of not running out of money over 30 years.
  • Lean vs. Fat: 'LeanFIRE' targets a minimalist budget (<$40k/yr) to retire fast. 'FatFIRE' targets a luxurious budget (>$100k/yr) requiring a larger portfolio.
  • Flexibility is Key: The math assumes a rigid withdrawal. If you are willing to cut spending during market crashes or work part-time, your required number drops significantly.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 4% Rule comes from the 'Trinity Study' based on US stock/bond returns. However, early retirees (40-50 years duration) often aim for a safer 3.5% withdrawal rate (roughly 28-30x expenses) to account for the longer timeline and US healthcare costs.

Calculating Your Freedom

Stop guessing. Run your personal numbers.

Step 1: Determine Annual Burn

Track every dollar for 12 months. Do not guess.
Example: You spend $60,000 per year (including taxes and insurance).

Step 2: The Multiple

Standard FIRE (25x): $60,000 x 25 = $1.5 Million.
Conservative FIRE (30x): $60,000 x 30 = $1.8 Million.
Why Conservative? If you retire at 35, your money needs to last 50+ years, not 30. The 4% rule was designed for a 30-year retirement.

Step 3: Adjust for Future Spending

Will your spending drop (paid off mortgage)? Or rise (travel/healthcare)?
If your mortgage ($20k/yr) will be paid off right before you retire, your post-FIRE spending is only $40,000.
New Target: $40,000 x 25 = $1 Million.

The Path to the Number

  1. Increase Savings Rate: Your savings rate (not income) determines your speed. Saving 10% takes 51 years. Saving 50% takes 17 years. Saving 70% takes 8.5 years.
  2. The 'Coast' Checkpoint: Once you hit ~50% of your FIRE number, you might be 'Coast FIRE'. This means your existing investments will grow to your full number by age 65 without further contributions. You can stop saving and just cover daily bills.
  3. Asset Location: You need money accessible before 59.5. Prioritize Taxable Brokerage accounts and Roth IRA contributions (which can be withdrawn penalty-free).

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Social Security count?

Yes, but it kicks in late. FIRE requires you to self-fund the gap between age 40 and 62. Social Security acts as 'Longevity Insurance' for your later years.

What about inflation?

The 4% rule is designed to account for inflation. You increase your withdrawal dollar amount by the CPI each year to maintain purchasing power.

Should I include home equity?

No. You cannot buy groceries with your kitchen. Your FIRE number is your Liquid Invested Assets (Stocks/Bonds). Home equity reduces your expenses (no rent), but isn't part of the 4% withdrawal pool.
